pepper_bell_bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of pepper foliage and fruit that spreads rapidly in warm, wet, humid conditions and via splashing water.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown with a yellow halo
Spots may merge, causing large dead patches and leaf drop
Raised, scab-like brown spots on fruit surface
Reduced marketable yield due to fruit blemishes
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Avoid working in fields when foliage is wet
Rotate crops away from peppers/tomatoes for at least 1-2 years
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant
Space plants for good airflow

chemical: Copper hydroxide combined with mancozeb (per label)

safety_notes: This system does not provide dosages — follow the product label and local extension guidance
Bacterial diseases do not respond to fungicides alone; confirm diagnosis before treating
Wear gloves and a mask when spraying

pepper_bell_healthy.description: No disease symptoms detected on this bell pepper leaf.
prevention: Continue routine field monitoring
Maintain balanced fertilization and consistent watering
Scout for early pest activity (aphids, thrips) that can transmit disease
safety_notes: This is an automated visual assessment, not a substitute for regular field inspection

potato_early_blight.description: A fungal disease of potato foliage and tubers, closely related to tomato early blight, most damaging to stressed or nutrient-deficient plants.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric ring patterns on lower leaves
Yellow halo surrounding lesions
Leaves become brittle and drop prematurely
Dark, sunken, dry lesions on tubers with slightly raised borders
prevention: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants for at least 2 years
Maintain balanced soil fertility — nitrogen-stressed plants are more susceptible
Avoid overhead watering; irrigate early in the day if unavoidable
Hill soil properly to reduce tuber exposure to spores

organic: Compost tea foliar applications to support plant immune response

safety_notes: Follow product label instructions strictly — no dosage recommendations are given here
Observe pre-harvest intervals before consuming treated tubers
Consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra or agricultural extension office

potato_late_blight.description: The same pathogen responsible for the historic Irish potato famine; remains one of the most economically damaging potato diseases worldwide.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale to dark green lesions on leaf tips and edges
Lesions quickly turn brown to black and expand rapidly
White fungal growth visible on leaf undersides in humid weather
Reddish-brown dry rot inside infected tubers
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Plant resistant varieties where available
Improve field drainage and avoid excess irrigation
Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants that can harbor spores over winter

organic: Preventive copper-based fungicide applications before wet weather periods
chemical: Fungicides containing mandipropamid, chlorothalonil, or cymoxanil, applied preventively

safety_notes: This disease can devastate a field within days — early reporting to an extension officer is critical
This system does not provide dosages; follow local agricultural authority guidance
Destroy severely infected plants to prevent spread to healthy fields

potato_healthy.description: No disease symptoms detected on this potato leaf.
prevention: Continue regular field monitoring for early symptom detection
Maintain balanced irrigation and fertilization
Practice crop rotation as a preventive measure even when no disease is present
safety_notes: This is an automated visual assessment, not a substitute for regular field inspection

tomato_bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease affecting tomato leaves, stems, and fruit, favored by warm, humid, rainy weather and overhead irrigation.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo
Spots on stems and fruit that may become raised and scab-like
Severe infections cause defoliation and reduced fruit quality
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Avoid overhead watering and working with wet plants
Rotate crops away from tomatoes/peppers for 1-2 seasons
Sanitize tools and stakes between uses

chemical: Copper hydroxide + mancozeb combination sprays (per label)

safety_notes: Bacterial spot does not respond to standard fungicides — confirm diagnosis before treating
This system does not provide dosages; follow the product label and local extension guidance

tomato_early_blight.description: A common fungal disease affecting tomato foliage, stems, and fruit, typically appearing on older, lower leaves first and progressing upward.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots on lower/older leaves
Spots develop concentric rings, giving a 'target board' appearance
Yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf tissue surrounding spots
Premature leaf drop, starting from the bottom of the plant
Dark, sunken lesions may appear on stems and fruit
prevention: Rotate crops — avoid planting tomatoes/potatoes in the same soil for 2-3 years
Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Space plants adequately to improve air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
Mulch around the base of plants to reduce soil splash onto leaves

organic: Copper-based fungicides, applied per product label

safety_notes: Always follow the product label for dosage and pre-harvest intervals — this system does not provide dosages
Wear appropriate protective equipment when applying any fungicide
Consult your local agricultural extension office before applying chemical treatments
Rotate fungicide classes to avoid resistance buildup

tomato_late_blight.description: An aggressive water-mold disease capable of destroying entire tomato and potato crops within days under cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked greenish-black lesions on leaves
White, fuzzy fungal growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of foliage
Dark, firm, greasy-looking lesions on fruit
Distinct musty odor from severely infected plants
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation and excess humidity around plants
Ensure good airflow through proper spacing and pruning
Monitor weather — risk increases sharply in cool, wet, humid conditions
Destroy volunteer potato/tomato plants which can harbor the pathogen

organic: Copper-based fungicides applied preventively before disease onset
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to slow spread

safety_notes: Late blight spreads extremely fast — isolate/remove infected plants immediately
This system does not provide dosages; follow local agricultural guidance
Consult a plant pathologist or extension officer for confirmation, as late blight can be confused with other blights

tomato_leaf_mold.description: A fungal disease most common in humid greenhouse conditions, primarily affecting leaves and rarely fruit.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grayish-brown velvety mold on the leaf underside, opposite the yellow spots
Leaves curl, wither, and drop in severe cases
prevention: Improve ventilation, especially in greenhouses/polyhouses
Reduce humidity around foliage; avoid overhead watering
Space and prune plants for airflow
Use resistant varieties where available
safety_notes: This system does not provide dosages; follow the product label
Humidity control is often more effective than spraying for this disease

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.description: A fungal disease that starts on lower, older leaves and can quickly spread upward, causing significant defoliation if untreated.
symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark brown margins and gray/tan centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) visible within the spot centers
Spots are numerous and can merge, causing yellowing and leaf drop
Fruit is rarely affected directly, but yield drops from reduced foliage
prevention: Rotate crops; avoid planting tomatoes in the same spot each year
Remove lower infected leaves and plant debris promptly
Avoid overhead watering; mulch to reduce soil splash
Space plants for good air circulation

organic: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves

safety_notes: This system does not provide dosages; follow local extension guidance
Start preventive sprays early in wet seasons — this disease progresses quickly once established

tomato_spider_mites_two_spotted_spider_m.description: A tiny sap-sucking pest (not a fungal/bacterial disease) that thrives in hot, dry conditions and can rapidly damage foliage.
symptoms: Fine yellow/white stippling or speckling on leaves
Leaves take on a bronzed or dusty appearance
Fine webbing visible on the underside of leaves and between stems in heavy infestations
Leaf curling and drop under severe infestation
prevention: Keep plants well-watered — mites thrive under drought stress
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, which favors mite reproduction
Encourage natural predators (predatory mites, ladybirds) by minimizing broad-spectrum insecticide use
Regularly hose down foliage to disrupt mite colonies

organic: Insecticidal soap or neem oil sprays, targeting leaf undersides
Introduce predatory mites (e.g. Phytoseiulus persimilis) where feasible
chemical: Miticides labeled specifically for spider mites (rotate active ingredients to avoid resistance)

safety_notes: This system does not provide dosages; follow the product label
General insecticides often make mite problems worse by killing natural predators

tomato_target_spot.description: A fungal disease producing concentric-ring lesions similar to early blight, affecting leaves, stems, and fruit in warm, humid climates.
symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric rings (target-like appearance) on leaves
Lesions may also appear on stems and fruit as sunken, dark spots
Severe infection causes extensive defoliation
prevention: Rotate crops and avoid dense planting
Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest
Avoid overhead irrigation and prolonged leaf wetness
Use resistant varieties where available
safety_notes: This system does not provide dosages; follow the product label and local guidance
Can be visually confused with early blight — confirm with a local expert if uncertain

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.description: A viral disease transmitted by whiteflies that can cause severe stunting and yield loss, especially in young plants.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaflet margins
Marked stunting of plant growth
Flower drop and drastically reduced fruit set
Smaller, misshapen leaves overall
prevention: Control whitefly populations (the virus's insect vector) with sticky traps and reflective mulches
Use virus-resistant tomato varieties where available
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce virus reservoir
Use insect-proof netting on nurseries/seedbeds

organic: No cure once infected — focus on whitefly control (yellow sticky traps, neem oil against whiteflies)
chemical: Insecticides targeting whiteflies (not the virus itself) — rotate modes of action to prevent resistance

safety_notes: There is no direct chemical cure for the virus itself — management targets the whitefly vector
This system does not provide dosages; consult local extension services for approved insecticides
Remove infected plants promptly to protect the rest of the field

tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A highly stable, easily spread viral disease affecting leaves and fruit quality, often transmitted mechanically through handling and tools.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled/mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion, curling, and fern-like narrowing in severe cases
Stunted plant growth
Mottled or uneven ripening on fruit
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed and resistant varieties
Disinfect tools, hands, and stakes between plants (this virus spreads easily by contact)
Avoid tobacco use/handling near plants (the virus is related to tobacco mosaic virus)
Remove and destroy infected plants promptly

organic: No cure once infected — remove and destroy infected plants
Sanitize tools and hands between plants to prevent spread
chemical: No chemical cure exists for viral infections — focus entirely on prevention and sanitation

safety_notes: There is no curative treatment for viral infections — this system's chemical/organic lists here focus on containment, not cure
Wash hands and disinfect tools between handling infected and healthy plants
